display_title: Official Review of Paper614 by Reviewer 5Pst

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors of the paper propose a novel loss function called Edit-Invariant Sequence Loss (EISL) which is a matching loss between reference n-gram and all n-gram in candidate sequence (generated sequence). It is motivated from that cross-entropy loss penalizes valid sentences but not exactly matched with the target sentence such as paraphrases. They empirically show that the model trained with the proposed loss function is robust to noise in the target sentence or weak supervision such as unsupervised text style transfer.
content.main_review:
## Pros
- The paper is well motivated in that it tackles limitation of cross entropy (CE) loss in text generation. CE penalizes many possible paraphrases and fragile to noisy reference sentences. The authors propose alternative loss function that is invariant to the shift of the positions, assuming that reordering of n-gram does not change the semantics of original sentence.

- The proposed method is simple and easy to implement with existing libraries.

- They verify their method with solid experimental results. Especially, the results from noisy machine translation and non-autoregressive generation is impressive.

- They derive upper bound of the marginalized n-gram matching loss, which enables trackable compuatation.

## Cons

-There is extra computational cost for the proposed loss function, but there is no explanation.

- Needs some hyperparameters to be tuned such as how long do we need to train the model with 
 n-gram with teacher forcing and which n-gram to use and their weights 
.

- A shift translation of subsequence in text highly likely leads to grammatically wrong sentences, which might degrades the quality of generation. The authors have performed human evaluation for generated text in style transfer experiment. In my opinion, however, it cannot explain why the model trained with the proposed loss function does not generate grammatically wrong sentences.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think the proposed method is well motivated and interesting. Moreover it is easy to implement and effective method when the signal from supervision is noisy. But I do not understand how the proposed method prevent the model to generate grammatically wrong sentences even the shift translation of subsequence might result in sentences with grammatical errors. If the authors clearly address my concern,  I will raise my score.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5Pst
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments!

* **Extra computational cost**
    
    Thanks for the comment. We've added detailed efficiency analysis to the new **Appendix A.4** section, including both the computation complexity analysis and the quantitative empirical comparisons of computing cost. In particular, **(1)** the computation cost of loss evaluation (either CE or EISL) is usually negligible compared to the cost of model forward and backward during training, as shown in Figure.9 in Appendix A.4. Besides, **(2)** as in practice we first pre-train the model with the CE loss and then fine-tune with the EISL loss, we also report the total time cost of both the pretraining and fine-tuning stages. From Table.7 in Appendix A.4, we can see that the time cost of the EISL fine-tuning is only around *30\%* of that of the CE pre-training while bringing substantial performance improvement.

* **Hyperparameters to be tuned**

    We've mentioned in the paper (the end of pp.4) that the hyperparameters all have effective default values as shown in our experiments. To make it clearer, we've added a new **Appendix A.5** section to discuss the hyperparameter selections. 

  Specifically,  most of the experiments (text style transfer and NAT) have simply used the default values $n\in\{2,3,4\}$ and equal weights $w_n=1/3$ for $n$-grams and achieved consistent substantial improvement over baselines. (In the noisy MT in section 4.1 we show the effect of different $n$-grams including those selected using the validation set). Besides, we don't need to tune the iteration of CE pretraining, since we simply do the CE pretraining **until convergence** before switching to the EISL fine-tuning.

* **Generating grammatically correct sentences** 

    We highlight that it is EISL's insensitivity to shift translation that facilitates the model to correctly learn to generate grammatical text **when the training data is noisy or weak**. The intuition is illustrated in Figure.1, as well as explained in **Appendix A.3.3** where we analyzed a concrete NAT example showcasing why EISL is superior to CE for generating grammatically correct sentences. 

  For instance, given a noisy training target $y_{noise}$, CE training forces the model to copy all tokens including errors in the target. The model is prevented from generating the grammatically correct sequence $y_{correct}$ since CE assigns a *high* loss to it, *even though $y_{correct}$ better fits the language pattern of the whole dataset*. In contrast, EISL is less sensitive to sequence edits, meaning that EISL assigns only a *mild* loss when the model generates $y_{correct}$ (see Figure.2). This offers the model a chance to deviate from $y_{noise}$ and generate $y_{correct}$ (to better fit the language pattern) since the loss of deviating from $y_{noise}$ is just *mild* and thus *affordable*.
 
  The above intuition has been empirically validated by the superior performance of EISL in the noisy-target, weak-target, and NAT settings, respectively, as shown in our experiments. The case studies in Appendix A.3.3 (for NAT), Appendix A.2.1 (for text style transfer), and the new Appendix A.7 (for noisy MT) further illustrate the effect of EISL for generating grammatical text. 

Please let us know if you have any more questions.

display_title: Official Review of Paper614 by Reviewer 2bw3

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Cross entropy loss is often undesirable for training sequence generation models, since it is not robust to small errors in generated sequences. The likelihood is pushed down for all sequences besides the training sequence, regardless of how similar they are to the target sequence. 

This paper introduces an approach for treating the target sequence as a bag of ngrams, where the loss penalizes differences between target ngram counts and expected ngram counts. This can be approximated using samples from the model at train time. Unlike RL approaches to minimize, for example, BLEU, this does not rely on score function estimators so it is better behaved in practice.

The performance improvement is noteworthy on a few NLP tasks.
content.main_review:
=Major Comments=

Most importantly, I'm unconvinced that the loss function is computing the desired quantity. The P matrix defined in the paragraph above (7) is defined by sampling the full sequence y' from the model. Here, each column is P(y'_i | y'<i). The convolution operation is computing the sum of the conditional probability of y^*_{i:i+n} occurring given y'_{<i}, across values of  i. However, the model is a fully-connected autoregressive model. To compute P(y^*_{i:i+n} | y_{<i}), we require that a forward pass in the model has been computed from position i to i+n using values from y*, not y'. Therefore, P does not have the right conditional probabilities, and there is no way to parallelize this across i.

Second, I do not have enough background on contemporary benchmarks in NLP to understand if the benchmark datasets and baselines are a good choice. Hopefully some other reviewer will know this, and if not I can ask some colleagues. 


=Minor Comments=
You penalize the negative log expected number of occurrences of an ngram. Does the loss behave reasonably if an ngram occurs multiple times in the ground truth sequence? 
I didn't follow why the 

The training cost will depend on the number of train-time samples. Do you have any results on how accuracy changes based on the number of samples?

Can you explain in more detail what this means? "We apply sequence-level knowledge distillation to the dataset, which can reduce the complexity of the dataset, making it easier for the model to learn and improving the performance."

Third, consider an RL formulation for the problem where the reward at step i is the fraction of target ngrams that have been generated so far. This could be trained with policy gradients, with per-step rewards. This differs from prior work that only considers a final reward (e.g., BLEU) after the entire sequence is generated. I think the objective function for that problem formulation and your problem formulation would be similar. Can you comment?


==After author's response==
See discussion thread below. The authors agree with me that the equations regarding P were incorrect. The paper text will need to be changed considerably to address this. While the empirical results are strong, the paper will need another full round of review at another conference to make sure that these changes are made appropriately.
content.summary_of_the_review: I have a critical question around whether the parallelized version of the loss computation based on convolutions is actually computing the right thing. Otherwise, I found the empirical results satisfying. I am assigning a weak reject, and will raise to a higher score if it turns out that I was wrong about the loss.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2bw3
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful comments! We address your questions below:

=Major Comments=

* **Computation of $P$ matrix**

    Thanks for the great question! We have updated the *Efficient Computation: EISL as Convolution* part in **Section 3.2** (highlighted in red) and added a new **Appendix A.8** section in response to your comment. Briefly, the computation is *exact* for a non-autoregressive generation model (e.g., as in the NAT experiments). For an autoregressive model, as you commented, the computation based on convolution indeed involves *approximation* (i.e., we replaced the $y^*_{i:i+n}$ with $y_{i':i'+n}$ when evaluating the conditionals). In the updated Section 3.2, we provide more clarification and highlight that the approximation is reasonable and effective, especially due to the *position selection* that (softly) picks those conditionals that tend to be well approximated.

  Further, in Appendix A.8, we show empirical evidence that the approximation is effective, by showing that our approximate loss is close to the exact loss during training (e.g., with very similar loss tendency), while being significantly faster to compute thanks to the convolution-based implementation. 
  
  We're happy to discuss more if you have more questions.
 
- **Benchmark datasets and baselines** 

    We'd like to highlight that the datasets used in our experiments are all the most popular benchmarks for respective tasks. Specifically, for the noisy machine translation and non-autoregressive translation tasks, we used *Multi30k de-en* and *WMT* datasets, which are the common standard datasets for MT research (e.g., please see [url1](http://www.statmt.org/wmt18/papers.html),[url2](http://www.statmt.org/wmt16/papers.html) and [url3](http://www.statmt.org/wmt14/papers.html) for lists of papers using *WMT* for MT study). For the text style transfer task, we used *Yelp review* and *Political* datasets, which are the first and most widely used datasets for the task (e.g., please refer to the latest survey paper ([Jin et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.00416)) for more details). 

  Besides, in each of the three tasks, we've compared with a wide range of the latest baselines (both in the paper and appendix) and shown consistent improvement of our approach across the tasks/baselines. 


=Minor Comments=

* **An n-gram occurs multiple times in GT**

    Our loss can properly handle an $n$-gram that occurs multiple times in the ground-truth target. Specifically, as described in the *Position Selection* paragraph (section 3.2), we sample (softly with Gumbel-softmax) multiple positions in the candidate to match the multiple occurrences of the $n$-gram, respectively.
        
* **Relationship between accuracy and number of training samples** 
    
    *Figure.6* in Section 4.1 shows how the accuracy changes as the number of training samples increases on the WMT dataset. We can see that, compared to the baselines, our EISL can make better use of the increasing training samples to improve the performance.

* **Clarification on knowledge distillation** 

    This is a **standard training setting** in the NAT task (e.g., see *[Zhou et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02727): Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation*). Specifically, one feeds the original training data into a pretrained autoregressive model (i.e., teacher model), and collects the model outputs as the training targets for training the non-autoregressive model of interest. We highlight that to ensure a fair comparison, our experimental setup including the knowledge distillation setting is exactly the same as in previous work.

* **Relation to the RL formulation**

    Thank you for the interesting thoughts! We agree that the RL formulation with the per-step rewards you described shares the similar intuition of our formulation, both aiming to improve the "coverage" of target n-grams. Yet we expect the RL approach could be less inefficient to train---there are indeed similar previous attempts that use *per-step* BLEU-style rewards (e.g., [Ding et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09346)) which however still has difficulty in efficient training ([Keneshloo et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.09461)). As discussed in the Introduction section (2nd paragraph in pp.2), due to large action space, policy gradient suffers from high variance (with either per-step or sequence-level reward). In contrast, the proposed EISL loss as a differentiable loss directly uses *gradient* to guide the model updates (thus similar to CE) and thus is more efficient. We'd be happy to discuss more.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a novel Edit-Invariant Sequence Loss (EISL), which is robust to various noises in the target sequence. Specifically, EISL computes the matching loss of a target n-gram with all n-grams in the generated sequence, which captures the edit invariance properties of text n-grams. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, the authors conducted experiments on three weak supervision tasks, i.e, machine translation, unsupervised text style transfer, and non-autoregressive generation.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- The motivation of the work is clear, the idea is intuitive and the proposed approach has been described clearly.
- The proposed approach is very interesting, and it provides a new perspective for investigating sequence training with noisy targets.
- The experiments are conducted on three tasks and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Weakness:
- The experiment lacks comparisons with some recent baselines, e.g., “CALCS: Continuously Approximating Longest Common Subsequence for Sequence Level Optimization” and “Improved Natural Language Generation via Loss Truncation”.
- The experimental metrics for non-autoregressive generation and machine translation tasks are only BLEUs. They are more easily captured by the ELSL than CE loss.
- Lack of efficiency analysis.
- More case studies should be added in the appendix to illustrate the benefit of the proposed method.

Questions & Recommendations:
- As shown in Figure 5(e), what is the reason that the performance of using lower grams is always better than higher grams?
- It would be good if the authors could report the quantitative results of the time complexity.
- In section A.2.1, there is an unfinished case study description.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper proposes a simple yet effective technique. The proposed technique has been described clearly, the idea is intuitive. It would be good to see the authors add more analysis on experiment results and also compare with more baselines.

content.title: Response to Reviewer iuYx (Part II)
content.comment:
* **More evaluation metrics**

    We reported BLEU as it is so far still the most widely used metric in previous non-autoregressive generation and machine translation research. As suggested by the reviewer, here we additionally report results using the latest model-based metric, **BLEURT** ([Sellam et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04696)), which has shown state-of-the-art strong correlation with human judgment on various tasks. The metric is based on a finetuned BERT model, taking as inputs a generated text and a reference, and computing a score measuring the fluency and semantic similarity of the generation w.r.t the reference. The metric thus does not favor either EISL or CE by design.

  We report the full BLEURT results on the noisy MT and non-autoregressive MT tasks in the new **Appendix A.6** section. We can see that EISL consistently outperforms baselines in terms of BLEURT, leading to the same conclusion as measured by BLEU.

* **Efficiency analysis** 

    Thanks for the suggestion! We've added detailed efficiency analysis to the new **Appendix A.4** section, including both the computation complexity analysis and the quantitative empirical comparisons of computing cost. In particular, **(1)** the computation cost of loss evaluation (either CE or EISL) is usually negligible compared to the cost of model forward and backward during training, as shown in Figure.9 in Appendix A.4. Besides, **(2)** as in practice we first pre-train the model with the CE loss and then fine-tune with the EISL loss, we also report the total time cost of both the pretraining and fine-tuning stages. From Table.7 in Appendix A.4, we can see that the time cost of the EISL fine-tuning is only around half of that of the CE pre-training while bringing substantial performance improvement.


* **More case studies**

    Thanks for the suggestion. Besides the existing qualitative analysis of text style transfer (Appendix A.2.1) and NAT (Appendix 3.3), now we added more case analysis in the new **Appendix A.7** section for noisy MT. We can see that even with noisy target data for training, EISL can preserve content and achieve grammar correctness to a great extent, while CE tends to fail. We show an example below:

    ```
    CE output: young man is running on a a and the other man is smiling .
    EISL output: young man is running in a dirt course and the other is smiling .
    ```
* **Lower grams perform better in Figure.5(e)** 

    Thanks for the nice question. Lower-gram EISL is less sensitive to noise. For example, $1$-gram EISL focuses mostly on matching individual tokens without caring much about the order of tokens; while a high-gram EISL (e.g., consider the extreme case of $T^*$-gram where $T^*$ is the target length) reduces to CE (as discussed in section 3.3) and is highly sensitive to noise. Thus, in the presence of high data noise, lower-gram EISL would be more robust and perform better. 

  Besides, on *low-noise* data (e.g., noise-level = 0 or 1), lower-gram EISL performs comparably with higher-gram EISL, both close to the CE performance. This is because we pretrained the model with CE (as mentioned in the experimental setup), and finetuning with EISL (either with lower- or higher-grams) would not change the performance a lot given the low-noise data. 

* **Unfinished case study description** 

    Thanks for pointing it out. We've completed the missing part in *Appendix A.2.1*. We'll fix all typos and polish them in the revised version.

Did you experiment with multiple iterations? It would strengthen the argument if the improvement still remains with more iterations, which is probably a more reasonable downstream application of these models.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ASST
content.comment:
Thank you for appreciating that our method is well-motivated and the improvements are substantial and convincing. 

We'd like to clarify that the experiments suggested by the reviewer are indeed already included in the paper and appendix, as we explain in more detail below: 

* **Comparison with prior work**

  We've already compared wih various strong NAT baselines in Section 4.3 and **Appendix A.3.2**, including *Bag-of-ngrams* loss ([Shao et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.09320)) as suggested by the reviewer, as well as *Auxiliary Regularization* ([Wang et al., 2019a](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10245)), *Hint-based Training* ([Li et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.06708)), and *Aligned Cross-Entropy* ([Ghazvininejad et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.01655)), etc. 

  Our approach achieves consistent improvement. For example, our approach (BLEU=24.17) is substantially better than *Bag-of-ngrams* ([Shao et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.09320), BLEU=20.90). Compared to *Bag-of-ngrams*, our method is **(1)** principally formulated (as an upper bound of the negative log expected value of $C(\mathbf y_{i:i+n}^*,\mathbf y)$, Eq.(2)); **(2)** with the derived position selection that avoids training collapse by preventing assigning equal probabilities at all positions; and **(3)** generally applicable to diverse text generation tasks beyond NAT as shown in our experiments.
  
  We did not compare with LAVA NAT ([Li et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.03084)) because the main difference of LAVA NAT lies in the model architecture, which is orthogonal to our method, i.e., a new loss function. (The training loss of  LAVA NAT is the standard combination of previous bag-of-words and CE losses.) Besides, as a preprint paper, LAVA NAT ([Li et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.03084)) lacks publically available code, while we had difficulty reproducing its results.


* **Experiments with NAT multiple iterations**

  We've already discussed and compared with multi-iteration NAT models in Section 4.3 and **Appendix A.3.1**. Specifically, Figure 7 in the appendix shows the effect of iteration steps. With increasing iteration steps, the difference in performance tends to fade away. We'd like to highlight that, as studied in [Kasai et al., (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10369), iterative NAT models do not hold the intrinsic advantage of speed when using many decoding iterations because Transformer baselines with a shallow decoder can easily achieve comparable speedup only at the sacrifice of minor performance drop. We thus have focused our empirical study on the setting of single iteration in Section 4.3.

content.title: General response to all reviewers
content.comment: We thank all reviewers for their insightful and encouraging comments. We're encouraged by the reviewer's appreciation that **(1)** our motivation is clear and intuitive (i.e., to overcome the problem of the popular cross-entropy training in sequence generation) (*R-ASST, R-iuYx, R-5Pst*), **(2)** the proposed method is simple yet effective, providing a new and interesting perspective for sequence training (*R-iuYx*), with well-derived formulation and is easy-to-implement (*R-5Pst*); **(3)** the empirical improvement is impressive, substantial, convincing, and satisfying (*R-ASST, R-iuYx, R-2bw3, R-5Pst*); and **(4)** the writing is clear (*R-iuYx*).
